chunks: And from him, from Amr ibn Uthman, from Hanan ibn Sadir, from his father, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the fasting of the Day of 'Arafah, and I said, 'May I be your ransom, they claim that it equals the fasting of a year.' He said, 'My father (peace be upon him) did not fast it.' I said, 'And why is that?' He said, 'Indeed, the Day of 'Arafah is a day of supplication and asking (of needs), and I fear that it will weaken me from supplication, and I dislike that I fast it, and I fear that 'Arafah might be the Day of Sacrifice (Eid al-Adha), so it is not a day of fasting.'

Thus, the way to reconcile between these narrations is that whoever is strong enough to fast this day without it preventing him from supplication, then it is recommended for him to fast this day. And whoever fears weakness and what prevents him from supplication and asking, then it is preferable for him to leave fasting it. And that which clarifies what we mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.يَعْدِلُ صَوْمَ سَنَةٍ: Equals the fasting of a year

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali (peace be upon him) avoid fasting on the Day of 'Arafah?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) clarifies that Imam Ali (peace be upon him) abstained from fasting on the Day of 'Arafah not due to dislike, but to preserve the physical strength necessary for extensive supplication (du'a), which is the day's primary spiritual objective. This establishes a nuanced Shia legal principle where the recommendation of fasting is conditional upon the individual's capacity to engage in worship without detriment, prioritizing the quality of devotion over the mere act of fasting.
